source.title: Negative (and Positive) Circles in Signed Graphs: A Problem Collection

accepted.question_text: For a signed graph Σ, where each edge has sign + or − and a circle is negative when the product of its edge signs is negative, determine whether a specified edge e belongs to at least one negative chordless circle.
accepted.context_brief: negative chordless circle through an edge

evidence.quote: Qn. 4−. In Σ, is a certain edge e in a negative chordless circle? Ans. Unknown.

accepted.question_text: For a signed graph Σ, determine whether a specified edge e belongs to exactly one negative chordless circle.
accepted.context_brief: unique negative chordless circle through an edge

evidence.quote: Qn. 5−. In Σ, is a certain edge e in a unique negative chordless circle? Ans. Unknown.

accepted.question_text: Given a signed graph Σ and an edge e, determine whether the decision problem “e does not belong to any negative induced circle” lies in the complexity class NP.
accepted.context_brief: complexity of excluding negative induced circles

evidence.quote: Question 3.5. Is the question, “Does a given edge e in a signed graph Σ not belong to any negative induced circle?”, in the class NP?

accepted.question_text: Given a signed graph Σ and an edge e, determine whether the decision problem “e does not belong to any positive induced circle” lies in the complexity class NP.
accepted.context_brief: complexity of excluding positive induced circles

evidence.quote: Question 3.5. Is the question, “Does a given edge e in a signed graph Σ not belong to any negative induced circle?”, in the class NP?—and the same for a positive induced circle.

accepted.question_text: Characterize the signed graphs in which every pair of negative circles has at least two vertices in common; the paper calls such signed graphs quasibalanced.

evidence.quote: Qn. 4. Characterize the signed graphs in which any two negative circles have at least two vertices in common. I call them quasibalanced. Ans. Soon to be known [Z]; see Section 4.2. (Moderately hard.)

accepted.question_text: Characterize signed simple graphs that have no chordless negative circles, or equivalently no negative holes other than possibly triangles.

evidence.quote: Qn. 5. Characterize the signed simple graphs with no chordless negative circles. Or, with none other than triangles; i.e., no negative holes. Ans. ... In general the questions are hard.

accepted.question_text: Characterize signed simple graphs that have no chordless positive circles, or equivalently no chordless positive circles other than possibly triangles.

evidence.quote: Qn. 6. Characterize the signed simple graphs with no chordless positive circles. Or, with none other than triangles. Ans. ... the general questions are not at all easy.

accepted.question_text: Determine which properties of a signed graph Σ and of a negative or positive circle C with one or more chords guarantee that, after negatively subdividing positive edges and possibly switching the signature, the image of C becomes chordless or fails to become chordless.

evidence.quote: Qn. 7. What properties of Σ and C imply that a negative (or positive) circle C with one or more chords does or does not become chordless in Σ∼ after switching Σ.

accepted.question_text: For a signed graph Σ, determine the maximum number p−(Σ) of pairwise vertex-disjoint negative circles.

evidence.quote: Qn. 1−. Given Σ, what is the value of p−(Σ)? Ans. Unknown.

accepted.question_text: For a signed graph Σ, determine the maximum number p+(Σ) of pairwise vertex-disjoint positive circles.

evidence.quote: Qn. 1+. The same question for p+(Σ). Ans. Unknown.

accepted.question_text: Design an efficient method that, given a signed graph Σ, finds a maximum set of pairwise disjoint negative circles or a maximum set of pairwise disjoint positive circles.

evidence.quote: Qn. 2±. Find a maximum set of pairwise disjoint negative, or positive, circles. Ans. Unknown. This is simply a more demanding version of Question 1. An answer should be an efficient algorithm.

accepted.question_text: For a signed graph Σ, determine when the maximum number p′−(Σ) of pairwise edge-disjoint negative circles equals the frustration index l(Σ), and decide whether this equality always holds.
accepted.context_brief: edge-disjoint negative circle packing and frustration index

evidence.quote: Qn. 3−. That p′−(Σ) ≤ min(l(Σ), p′(|Σ|)) is obvious. When is there equality? Ans. Unknown.
Conjecture. There is always equality.

accepted.question_text: For a signed graph Σ, determine the maximum number p′+(Σ) of pairwise edge-disjoint positive circles.

evidence.quote: Qn. 3+. Evaluate p′+(Σ), given Σ. Ans. Unknown.

accepted.question_text: Design an efficient method that, given a signed graph Σ, finds a maximum set of pairwise edge-disjoint negative circles or a maximum set of pairwise edge-disjoint positive circles.

evidence.quote: Qn. 4±. Find a maximum set of pairwise edge-disjoint negative, or positive, circles. Ans. Unknown.

accepted.question_text: For a signed graph Σ, determine the minimum number of negative circles or positive circles needed to cover all vertices, and characterize or compute minimum such covering sets.

evidence.quote: Qns. 5–6±. Like Questions 1–2± but for the minimum number or minimum sets of negative (or positive) circles that cover all the vertices of Σ. Ans. Unknown.

accepted.question_text: For a signed graph Σ, determine the minimum number of negative circles or positive circles needed to cover all edges, and characterize or compute minimum such covering sets.

evidence.quote: Qns. 7–8±. Like Questions 5–6± but for circles that cover the edges of Σ. Ans. Unknown.

accepted.question_text: Determine whether there are meaningful duality relations between packing numbers and covering numbers for negative circles or positive circles in signed graphs.

evidence.quote: Qn. 9±. Are there duality relations between packing and covering numbers? Ans. Unknown.

accepted.question_text: Characterize the signed graphs Σ whose edge sets can be decomposed into negative circles.

evidence.quote: Qn. 10−. Which Σ can be decomposed into negative circles? Ans. Unknown.

accepted.question_text: Give a complete characterization of the signed graphs Σ whose edge sets can be decomposed into positive circles.

evidence.quote: Qn. 10+. Which Σ can be decomposed into positive circles? Ans. Partially known.

accepted.question_text: When a signed graph Σ admits a decomposition into negative circles or into positive circles, determine the smallest number of circles required in such a decomposition.

evidence.quote: Qn. 11−. If Σ can be decomposed into negative circles, what is the smallest number of circles it needs? Ans. Unknown.
Qn. 11+. If Σ can be decomposed into positive circles, what is the smallest number of circles? Ans. Unknown.

accepted.question_text: Identify an interesting property of a connected signed graph, analogous to the existence of an Eulerian tour in an unsigned graph, that corresponds to decomposability into negative circles or positive circles.

evidence.quote: Qn. 12±. Is there an interesting property of a connected signed graph, similar to existence of an Eulerian tour, related to decomposition into negative or positive circles? Ans. Unknown.

accepted.question_text: Suppose a signed graph Σ has a Hamiltonian circle and is unbalanced. Determine whether Σ must contain a negative Hamiltonian circle and whether it must contain a positive Hamiltonian circle.

evidence.quote: Qn. 1. Assume Σ has a Hamiltonian circle and is unbalanced. Is there a negative Hamiltonian circle? A positive one? Ans. Unknown.

accepted.question_text: Characterize the underlying graphs Γ with the property that every signature on Γ has both positive and negative circles of every length that occurs in Γ.
accepted.context_brief: all lengths realized in both signs

evidence.quote: Qn. 2. For which graphs Γ is it true that every signature σ has both positive and negative circles of every length that occurs in Γ? Ans. I know of nothing other than Popescu’s theorem.

accepted.question_text: Study structural questions about sign-specific circles in signed graphs: determine when there exists a positive or negative circle C such that deleting the edges of C leaves Σ disconnected, separable, 2-separable, or 2-connected, and determine what kinds of bridges or chord structures negative or positive circles can have in important classes of signed graphs.
accepted.context_brief: connectivity and bridge structure of signed circles

evidence.quote: Qn. 3. Is there a positive, or negative, circle C such that Σ \ E(C) is disconnected, or separable, or 2-separable, or 2-connected? ... Do these generalize to signed graphs, evenness generalizing to positivity?
Qn. 4. What are the bridges (in the sense of Tutte) of a negative or positive circle? For instance, does the circle have many chords?

accepted.question_text: Fix a graph Γ and a length k. Characterize the set C_k(Γ) of all possible numbers of negative circles of length k that can occur over all signatures of Γ.

evidence.quote: Qn. 1. Characterize the set of numbers of negative circles of some fixed length of all signatures of a fixed graph Γ; that is, the set Ck(Γ) = {c−k(Γ, σ) : σ is a signature of Γ} for some fixed k, 3 ≤ k ≤ n.

accepted.question_text: For a fixed graph Γ, understand the geometry and combinatorics of the set C(Γ) of negative circle vectors over all signatures of Γ: determine its dimension, describe the cone and convex hull generated by these vectors, find restrictions on which vectors can actually occur, and identify nonzero vectors that can be guaranteed to belong to C(Γ).

evidence.quote: Qn. 2. Characterize the set C(Γ) = {c−(Γ, σ) : σ is a signature of Γ} of negative circle vectors of signatures of Γ.
2a. What is the dimension of C? In particular, when is dim C = m, the largest it could be?

2b. What is the cone (with apex at the origin) generated by C? ... 2c. What is the convex hull conv C? ... 2d. What restrictions can one find for actual negative circle vectors? ... 2e. Are there vectors other than 0 that can easily be guaranteed to be in C?

accepted.question_text: Generalize the spectral existence results for odd and even cycles to signed graphs: determine for which signed simple graphs Nikiforov-type eigenvalue conditions force the existence of negative or positive circles, and determine whether the Yuan and Nikiforov–Yuan upper-bound theorems for forbidden odd or even cycle lengths extend to signed simple graphs with negative or positive circles of prescribed lengths.

evidence.quote: Qn. 1. Does Nikiforov’s theorem, with bipartiteness changed to balance, apply to all signed simple graphs that meet the conditions of the theorem of [N]. If not, to which ones does it apply?

Qn. 2. Do Yuan’s theorem and that of Nikiforov and Yuan generalize to signed simple graphs that meet conditions similar to those of their theorems, with C2k+1 replaced by a negative Cl and C2k changed to a positive Cl?

accepted.question_text: Characterize the signed digraphs in which every directed cycle is negative.
accepted.context_brief: signed digraphs with all cycles negative

evidence.quote: Qn. 3− In which signed digraphs are all cycles negative? Ans. The two articles I know of, [HLM, Ch], provide examples but the question remains open as far as I know.

accepted.question_text: For a signed digraph (D, σ), determine when the directed frustration index—the minimum number of edges whose deletion makes the digraph cycle balanced—equals the ordinary frustration index of the underlying undirected signed graph.

evidence.quote: Qn. 1− What is the directed frustration index l(D, σ), i.e., the smallest number of edges whose deletion results in cycle balance? ... therefore the directed frustration index is bounded above by the undirected frustration index l(Γ, σ), where Γ is the undirected underlying graph of D. Under what conditions are they equal?

accepted.question_text: For a signed digraph (D, σ), determine when the directed frustration number—the minimum number of vertices whose deletion makes the digraph cycle balanced—equals the ordinary frustration number of the underlying undirected signed graph.

evidence.quote: Qn. 2− What is the directed frustration number l0(D, σ), i.e., the smallest number of vertices whose deletion results in cycle balance? ... As with the index, the directed frustration number is bounded above by l0(Γ, σ). When are they equal?

accepted.question_text: For a signed digraph, determine the smallest number of edges that meet every positive directed cycle.
accepted.context_brief: edge cover for positive directed cycles

evidence.quote: Qn. 1+ What is the smallest number of edges that cover all positive cycles? (Reminder: Not necessarily all positive circles!)

accepted.question_text: For a signed digraph, determine the smallest number of vertices that meet every positive directed cycle.
accepted.context_brief: vertex cover for positive directed cycles

evidence.quote: Qn. 2+ What is the smallest number of vertices that cover all positive cycles?

needs_review.question_text_raw: Qn. 13+ If Σ can be decomposed into circles (that is, if all degrees are even), what is its circle negativity? ... Thus, I propose: Qn. 13− If Σ can be decomposed into circles (that is, if all degrees are even), what is its circle negativity?

evidence.quote: Qn. 13+ If Σ can be decomposed into circles (that is, if all degrees are even), what is its circle negativity?

There is the obvious complementary question about the circle positivity of Σ. ... Thus, I propose: Qn. 13− If Σ can be decomposed into circles (that is, if all degrees are even), what is its circle negativity?
